modules.title: Module 1: Introduction to Cybersecurity
modules.description: Foundations of information security, security concepts, and the modern threat landscape.

lessons.title: 1. What is Cybersecurity?
lessons.content: Cybersecurity is the practice of protecting systems, networks, devices, and data from digital attacks, damage, or unauthorized access. In this introductory lesson, we examine the primary motivations behind attacks, the economic impact of cyber crime, and foundational security hygiene.
learning_objectives: Define cybersecurity and its scope
Identify key components of digital infrastructure
Understand why cybersecurity is critical for modern organizations

lessons.title: 2. Information Security vs Cybersecurity
lessons.content: While often used interchangeably, Information Security (InfoSec) covers all data protection regardless of format (digital, paper, physical), whereas Cybersecurity specifically focuses on safeguarding electronic assets, networks, and internet-connected systems.
learning_objectives: Distinguish between InfoSec and CyberSec
Understand non-digital security controls

lessons.title: 3. CIA Triad
lessons.content: The Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability (CIA) Triad is the guiding benchmark model for security policy and architecture. Confidentiality prevents unauthorized disclosure, Integrity protects data from unauthorized alteration, and Availability guarantees access when needed.
learning_objectives: Analyze the three pillars of the CIA Triad
Map real-world security breaches to compromised CIA components

lessons.title: 4. Types of Cyber Threats
lessons.content: Explores nation-state actors, cybercriminals, hacktivists, insider threats, and script kiddies, analyzing their motivations, funding, and common tactics.
learning_objectives: Classify threat actors by skill level and motivation
Understand threat modeling basics

lessons.title: 5. Cybersecurity Roles and Career Paths
lessons.content: Overview of career paths including SOC Analyst, Penetration Tester, Security Engineer, Incident Responder, and Compliance Auditor.
learning_objectives: Understand career specializations and certifications in cybersecurity

modules.title: Module 2: Networking Fundamentals for Cybersecurity
modules.description: Essential network architecture, protocols, addressing, and perimeter defense.

lessons.title: 1. Introduction to Computer Networks
lessons.content: Understanding the OSI 7-Layer Model and TCP/IP 4-Layer Model. Packet encapsulation, decapsulation, and data flow through routers and switches.
learning_objectives: Navigate the OSI and TCP/IP models
Trace packet delivery across network boundaries

lessons.title: 2. IP Addresses and MAC Addresses
lessons.content: Deep dive into IPv4, IPv6, Subnet masks, Private vs Public IP ranges (RFC 1918), and Layer 2 Hardware MAC addresses.

lessons.title: 3. TCP vs UDP
lessons.content: Connection-oriented Transmission Control Protocol (TCP 3-way handshake: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) versus connectionless User Datagram Protocol (UDP).

lessons.title: 4. Ports and Protocols
lessons.content: Well-known ports (HTTP 80, HTTPS 443, SSH 22, DNS 53, FTP 21, SMTP 25, RDP 3389) and how port scanning works.

lessons.title: 5. HTTP and HTTPS
lessons.content: Cleartext HTTP request/response methods vs encrypted HTTPS utilizing TLS/SSL.

lessons.title: 6. DNS Fundamentals
lessons.content: Domain Name System resolution hierarchy, root servers, A records, CNAME, MX, and DNS cache poisoning risks.

lessons.title: 7. Firewalls and Network Security Basics
lessons.content: Stateful vs stateless firewalls, packet filtering rules, Network Address Translation (NAT), and basic IDS/IPS concepts.

modules.title: Module 3: Common Cyber Threats and Attacks
modules.description: Examine the most pervasive cyber attacks, malware variants, and social engineering methods.

lessons.title: 1. Malware Fundamentals
lessons.content: Definition and classifications of malicious software: delivery vectors, payloads, and persistence mechanisms.

lessons.title: 2. Viruses, Worms and Trojans
lessons.content: Self-replicating file infectors (viruses), self-propagating network worms, and deceptive Trojan horses.

lessons.title: 3. Phishing and Social Engineering
lessons.content: Spear phishing, whaling, vishing, smishing, pretexting, baiting, and psychological triggers exploited by attackers.

lessons.title: 4. Password Attacks
lessons.content: Brute force attacks, dictionary attacks, credential stuffing, password spraying, and rainbow table lookups.

lessons.title: 5. Denial-of-Service Attacks
lessons.content: SYN floods, UDP amplification, HTTP floods, and botnet-driven Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) mitigation.

lessons.title: 6. Man-in-the-Middle Attacks
lessons.content: ARP poisoning, DNS spoofing, rogue Wi-Fi access points, and SSL stripping.

lessons.title: 7. Ransomware
lessons.content: Double-extortion ransomware operations, encryption mechanisms, payment demands, and backup defense strategies.

lessons.title: 8. Real-World Attack Scenarios
lessons.content: Case study breakdown of historic breaches (Equifax, Target, SolarWinds) and lessons learned.

modules.title: Module 4: Authentication and Access Control
modules.description: Identity verification, access models, and authorization governance.

lessons.title: 1. Authentication Fundamentals
lessons.content: The three factors of authentication: Something you know, Something you have, Something you are.

lessons.title: 2. Password Security
lessons.content: Entropy, length vs complexity, NIST SP 800-63B password guidelines, and enterprise password managers.

lessons.title: 3. Multi-Factor Authentication
lessons.content: Time-based One-Time Passwords (TOTP), SMS OTP risks, push notifications, and FIDO2/WebAuthn hardware security keys.

lessons.title: 4. Authorization and Access Control
lessons.content: Discretionary Access Control (DAC), Mandatory Access Control (MAC), and Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC).

lessons.title: 5. Role-Based Access Control
lessons.content: Designing RBAC matrices, group inheritance, and avoiding role explosion in enterprise directories.

lessons.title: 6. Principle of Least Privilege
lessons.content: Enforcing minimum necessary permissions, Just-in-Time (JIT) access, and reducing attack surfaces.

lessons.title: 7. Session Security
lessons.content: HTTP cookies, Secure/HttpOnly flags, SameSite attributes, session fixation, and token expiration.

modules.title: Module 5: Cryptography Fundamentals
modules.description: Encryption, hashing algorithms, digital signatures, and public key infrastructure.

lessons.title: 1. What is Cryptography?
lessons.content: Historical ciphers to modern mathematical encryption. Protecting data-in-transit, data-at-rest, and data-in-use.

lessons.title: 2. Encryption vs Hashing
lessons.content: Two-way reversible encryption algorithms versus one-way deterministic cryptographic hash functions.

lessons.title: 3. Symmetric Encryption
lessons.content: Shared secret keys, AES-128/256, block cipher modes (GCM, CBC), and key distribution challenges.

lessons.title: 4. Asymmetric Encryption
lessons.content: Public and private key pairs, RSA, Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC), and Diffie-Hellman key exchange.

lessons.title: 5. Digital Signatures
lessons.content: Non-repudiation, hashing payloads and encrypting hashes with private keys to ensure document authenticity.

lessons.title: 6. SSL/TLS Basics
lessons.content: Certificate Authorities (CAs), X.509 certificates, TLS handshake negotiation, and certificate revocation lists.

lessons.title: 7. Password Hashing and Salting
lessons.content: Salt generation, Argon2, bcrypt, PBKDF2, and mitigating rainbow table lookups.

modules.title: Module 6: Linux Security Basics
modules.description: Essential Linux security commands, file permissions, processes, and hardening.

lessons.title: 1. Introduction to Linux for Security
lessons.content: Filesystem hierarchy (/etc, /var/log, /home, /bin), bash shell navigation, and user context.

lessons.title: 2. Linux File Permissions
lessons.content: Read, write, execute (rwx) permissions, numeric chmod (755, 644, 600), chown, and SUID/SGID special bits.

lessons.title: 3. Users and Groups
lessons.content: Managing /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow files, useradd, usermod, and configuring sudoers privileges.

lessons.title: 4. Basic Security Commands
lessons.content: Hands-on usage of netstat/ss, lsof, uname, whoami, id, grep, and find commands for security audits.

lessons.title: 5. Processes and Services
lessons.content: Inspecting running processes with ps, top, htop, managing systemd services (systemctl), and kill signals.

lessons.title: 6. Logs and Monitoring
lessons.content: Reading /var/log/auth.log, /var/log/syslog, journalctl, and monitoring failed login attempts.

lessons.title: 7. Basic Linux Hardening
lessons.content: Disabling root SSH login, changing default ports, setting up UFW (Uncomplicated Firewall), and automatic security updates.

modules.title: Module 7: Vulnerability and Security Basics
modules.description: Vulnerability management, patch cycles, configuration audits, and risk assessment.

lessons.title: 1. What is a Vulnerability?
lessons.content: Flaws in software design, implementation, or configuration that can be exploited by an attacker.

lessons.title: 2. Vulnerability vs Threat vs Risk
lessons.content: Risk equation: Risk = Threat x Vulnerability x Impact. Performing qualitative risk evaluations.

lessons.title: 3. Security Misconfiguration
lessons.content: Default passwords, exposed admin panels, unencrypted communications, and unnecessary open ports.

lessons.title: 4. Software Updates and Patch Management
lessons.content: Patch Tuesday, zero-day vulnerabilities, staging updates, and enterprise patch deployment workflows.

lessons.title: 5. Basic Vulnerability Assessment
lessons.content: Introduction to vulnerability scanners (Nessus, OpenVAS, Nmap vulnerability scripts).

lessons.title: 6. Security Hardening
lessons.content: CIS Benchmarks, DISA STIGs, and minimizing attack surfaces on operating systems and applications.

lessons.title: 7. Security Best Practices
lessons.content: Data backups (3-2-1 rule), clean desk policy, security awareness training, and defense in depth.

modules.title: Module 8: Incident Response Fundamentals
modules.description: NIST and SANS incident handling lifecycle, triage, containment, and SOC team collaboration.

lessons.title: 1. What is Incident Response?
lessons.content: Organized approach to addressing and managing the aftermath of a security breach or cyberattack.

lessons.title: 2. Incident Detection
lessons.content: Identifying anomalies from IDS alerts, antivirus notifications, SIEM reports, and user escalations.

lessons.title: 3. Incident Analysis
lessons.content: Determining the scope, attack vector, impacted systems, and sensitivity of compromised data.

lessons.title: 4. Containment
lessons.content: Short-term isolation (network disconnection, firewall blocking) vs long-term system segmentation.

lessons.title: 5. Eradication and Recovery
lessons.content: Removing malware artifacts, closing vulnerabilities, restoring clean backups, and monitoring systems.

lessons.title: 6. Security Logs
lessons.content: Preserving chain of custody for log evidence, timestamp synchronization (NTP), and log integrity.

lessons.title: 7. Introduction to SOC Operations
lessons.content: Tier 1 Alert Triage, Tier 2 Incident Investigation, Tier 3 Threat Hunting, and SOC manager roles.

modules.title: Module 9: Practical Cybersecurity Scenarios
modules.description: Step-by-step practical simulations analyzing real-world security events.

lessons.title: 1. Identifying a Phishing Email
lessons.content: Hands-on analysis of email headers (SPF, DKIM, DMARC), spoofed sender addresses, suspicious links, and malicious attachments.

lessons.title: 2. Analyzing a Suspicious Login
lessons.content: Investigating impossible travel anomalies, foreign IP geolocation lookups, and multiple failed password attempts.

lessons.title: 3. Understanding a Malware Alert
lessons.content: Interpreting Windows Defender / EDR detection alerts, file hash lookups on VirusTotal, and quarantine procedures.

lessons.title: 4. Basic Log Analysis
lessons.content: Parsing Apache access logs and Windows Event Viewer logs to pinpoint brute force attacks.

assessment_questions.question_text: In modern JavaScript, what is the key difference between '==' and '===' operators?
options: There is no difference; they can be used interchangeably
'==' compares values with type coercion, whereas '===' compares both value and type without coercion
'===' is only used for strings and '==' is used for numbers
assessment_questions.explanation: '===' performs strict equality checking without type casting/coercion.

assessment_questions.question_text: Which HTTP status code signifies that a resource was successfully created on the server?
assessment_questions.explanation: HTTP 201 Created indicates that the request has succeeded and led to the creation of a resource.

assessment_questions.question_text: In React, why should state variables never be mutated directly (e.g. state.count = 5)?
options: Direct mutation breaks JavaScript memory allocation
Direct mutation prevents React from detecting state changes and triggering a re-render
Mutating state throws a fatal compile-time syntax error
React only allows state mutation inside the index.html file
assessment_questions.explanation: React relies on immutable state updates to compare references (shallow comparison) and re-render components.

assessment_questions.question_text: Which CSS Flexbox property controls alignment along the main axis?
assessment_questions.explanation: 'justify-content' aligns flex items along the main axis, while 'align-items' aligns along the cross axis.

assessment_questions.question_text: What is the primary function of an ORM (Object-Relational Mapping) library?
options: To compile JavaScript code into WebAssembly
To interact with database tables and records using object-oriented programming paradigms instead of raw SQL
To encrypt network traffic between client and server
To automate Git commits during deployment
assessment_questions.explanation: An ORM maps relational database tables to OOP models, simplifying queries and schema interactions.

assessment_questions.question_text: Which of the following is a classic Supervised Learning problem?
options: Predicting house prices based on square footage and location
Anomaly Detection in server logs without labeled fraud tags
assessment_questions.explanation: Supervised learning uses labeled target outputs (like historical house prices) to train predictive models.

assessment_questions.question_text: What symptom best describes an 'Overfitted' machine learning model?
options: Low training accuracy and low test accuracy
High training accuracy but poor generalization / low test accuracy
Equal high accuracy on both training and real-world unseen test data
The model trains too quickly on GPU
assessment_questions.explanation: Overfitting occurs when a model memorizes the noise in training data, causing high training score but poor test performance.

assessment_questions.question_text: When evaluating a medical disease detection model where missing a sick patient is dangerous, which metric should be prioritized?
assessment_questions.explanation: Recall minimizes False Negatives, ensuring as few sick patients as possible are missed.

assessment_questions.question_text: In Python Pandas, what does the .dropna() method do?
options: Deletes the entire DataFrame from memory
Removes rows or columns containing missing/NaN values
Fills missing values with the mean
Sorts the dataset in descending order
assessment_questions.explanation: .dropna() filters out rows or columns that contain null or NaN values.

assessment_questions.question_text: What is the role of an Activation Function in an Artificial Neural Network?
options: To save the model weights to the disk
To introduce non-linearity, enabling the network to learn complex patterns
To format input images into JPEG format
To reduce the number of CPU cores used
assessment_questions.explanation: Activation functions (like ReLU, Sigmoid) introduce non-linear transformations so networks can approximate non-linear functions.

assessment_questions.question_text: What is the key difference between Docker Containers and traditional Virtual Machines?
options: Containers require their own dedicated hypervisor and guest operating system
Containers share the host OS kernel and isolate processes, making them lighter and faster to start
Virtual Machines do not use any physical hardware resources
Docker containers can only run Python scripts
assessment_questions.explanation: Containers virtualize at the OS level and share the host kernel, whereas VMs virtualize physical hardware with separate guest OSs.

assessment_questions.question_text: What does CI/CD stand for in modern software development?
options: Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery / Continuous Deployment
assessment_questions.explanation: CI/CD is an automated pipeline workflow for frequent code integration, testing, and deployment.

assessment_questions.question_text: Which cloud principle involves automatically provisioning computing resources in response to fluctuating traffic?
assessment_questions.explanation: Auto Scaling dynamically expands or contracts compute instances to match current demand.

assessment_questions.question_text: In AWS, what type of storage service is Amazon S3?
assessment_questions.explanation: Amazon S3 is high-durability, scalable object storage designed for files, media, and data backups.

assessment_questions.question_text: What is the benefit of Infrastructure as Code (IaC) tools like Terraform?
options: Eliminates the need for writing application code
Enables declarative, reproducible, and version-controlled infrastructure provisioning
Automatically writes unit tests for frontend buttons
assessment_questions.explanation: IaC defines cloud infrastructure in configuration files that can be versioned, tested, and automatically provisioned.
